I am a single mother. As a child, I was molested by my mother's boyfriend. I never knew my father. I started having children at 18 right after high school. After having children, I completely lost myself and focused all my attention on my children. Now that my children are getting older, I still don't know myself. I've had several failed relationships after their father left me, which led me to feel depressed.

What you are experiencing is common for many mothers. It's typical to lose sight of oneself while focusing entirely on children and putting personal wants and needs aside. To help you begin to reconnect with yourself, I usually guide clients through a structured process. In our first session, we explore questions such as: What do I love (besides my children)? What are my own needs and desires? What are three accomplishments that make me proud? What five strengths or qualities do I possess? What significant event has impacted my life? How has that event affected me? As homework, I often ask clients to write a letter to themselves, expressing what they love, cherish, appreciate, and admire about themselves. Though it may feel uncomfortable at the start, it's important to remember that the more you value and love yourself, the more you can offer love and support to others.

I've always wanted to fix my issues, but I never get around to it. How can I change my feeling of being worthless to everyone?

You can definitely work on this... and the first step is to believe you are worthy TO YOURSELF. Recognizing that you are on a journey is already a significant first step. Taking the time to start exploring who you are is definitely the next. Approach this with self-compassion and kindness. Understand that this is a process, and just look forward to what you might discover. It may be helpful to find someone to talk to, as there are many supportive options available for your situation. Also, consider investing time and effort into this journey—YOU DESERVE IT. Have patience and take the first steps; the answers you seek are out there, and asking these questions already puts you on the right path.

I suggest that exploring these issues further with a therapist could help you address the stress, trouble sleeping, and frightening dreams.

Hello! I write to respond to your recent inquiry for possible increase in self-esteem and positive behavioral change regarding motivation for a new job. First of all, please try to allow yourself some time for grief over the loss of your dear grandmother. It appears you were close to her in many ways, and she had a great influence on your life. The grief process, which includes anger, denial, despair, and acceptance, may be a part of what is keeping you feeling 'stuck' in a cycle of not feeling motivated to find work at this time. Perhaps your mind is constantly fighting this grief? Death can be a traumatic experience for some people and is considered a great loss; thus, the grief process may continue to be a part of your world for a time, but hopefully not keep you 'stuck' in the long term. I would recommend reaching out to a counselor to discuss the grief process at a deeper level to discern whether her death is part of why you feel this way. Grief and loss can also have an effect on your self-esteem. Can you begin to see how this cycle is what you may be experiencing? One positive I see is that you are continuing to look for a new job! Take time to give yourself some credit for the time you are spending looking for work. Also, I would suggest setting some short-term goals, for example, making a list of 5-10 potential new employers and sending them each your resume. Then follow up soon with an email or call to ensure the hiring manager or human resources received your resume and to see if they have any questions. It is also a good idea to ask for informational interviews in order to get your foot in the door, so to speak. I hope that this information is helpful to you! Please let me know if you have any questions or concerns. Warmly, Atlas.

When faced with extreme stress, our bodies can enter a state of 'freeze,' which numbs emotional pain but also creates a disconnection from our feelings. This disconnection can persist until we begin to process the trauma. I encourage you to consider working with a therapist who specializes in trauma, who can guide you through evidence-based methods to help you reconnect with your emotions and regain a sense of fulfillment in life.

I'm in my late teens and live with my dad. The only time I go out is for my college classes. Sometimes when I see my friends I want to talk with them, but sometimes I won't want to talk to them for a while. Sometimes I feel like I'm not worth knowing or that I'm never going to do anything right. Am I depressed?

Hello. Being a teenager in today's society can create feelings of depression quite easily. It's common to internalize doubts about your ability to contribute or feel valued by those around you. You're also at a stage where you're trying to discover your identity and future direction, which can be overwhelming with the pressures of social judgment about appearances and popularity. It's important to recognize that many of the things that may seem critical now often won't matter as much in the long run. If you're feeling down because you lack some of the things that your peers hold as important, remember that qualities like kindness, compassion, and the effort to become a better person are far more significant. Depression can often be a symptom of underlying issues rather than a standalone problem, and identifying the triggers can be essential in managing your feelings. Have you had a chance to discuss your feelings with your dad or someone else you trust? It might also help to find a supportive friend or consider resources like peer counseling services that are available for teens. Don't hesitate to reach out for support; you're not alone in this journey, and there are people and services ready to help you navigate through these tough feelings.
